title: Scaling Thermal Analysis From Transistors To Data Centers
gist: A closed-door Design Automation Conference roundtable with Synopsys, Silvaco, Vinci, Keysight EDA and Siemens EDA argues heat has become an architectural constraint rather than a back-end check: hotspot prediction must move from three PVT corners to per-transistor resolution, packages with 20-25 chiplets force package- and system-level multi-physics, and ASIC thermals are hot enough to push HBM toward custom variants. The proposed toolchain is reduced-order models, surrogate/digital twins at chip, package and system level, and direct-coupled stress-thermal solvers, with agentic MCP flows raising auditability concerns.

insights.claim: Heat management has moved from a transistor-density question to an architectural decision, where how a design is packaged, how heat is moved away, how much heat density a chip can absorb, and what cooling is feasible with vertical integration are now primary architecture inputs.
insights.speaker: Satish Radhakrishnan, head of semiconductor and electronics, Vinci
insights.so_what: Thermal capability becomes a gating factor on which architectures can ship at all — watch it as a differentiator in accelerator roadmaps.
insights.quote: Thermal has shifted more toward an architectural discussion.
insights.locator: Big trade-offs in data centers — "Radhakrishnan: Thermal has shifted"

insights.claim: Designing for thermal means trading off power budget, floor plan, routing resources and timing budget simultaneously, because temperature changes delay, timing and power and feeds into signal integrity and warpage.
insights.speaker: Lang Lin, director of product management, Synopsys
insights.so_what: Thermal is now coupled to tapeout sign-off across multiple physics, expanding the EDA tool bundle a design team must license.
insights.locator: Big trade-offs in data centers — "Design for thermal involves trading off multi-physics factors"

insights.claim: The classical multi-physics trio traded off against each other is performance, mechanical and thermal, but reliability must be added as a fourth axis, and for high-reliability applications the floor-planning optimization becomes package size versus performance versus reliability.
insights.speaker: Chris Mueth, director of new markets management, Keysight EDA
insights.so_what: Reliability-constrained segments (auto, aerospace, hyperscale fleets) will pay for multi-physics tooling ahead of the broader market.
insights.locator: Big trade-offs in data centers — "For multi-physics, the big three"

insights.claim: Thermal analysis scope must extend from chip to package to board to system and out to the data center, because larger systems draw far more power and generate far more heat — yet chip-level work remains the most important lever since that is where heat originates.
insights.speaker: John Ferguson, senior director of product management, Siemens EDA
insights.so_what: EDA vendors are extending their TAM from die-level sign-off into data center-scale simulation — a new adjacent market to size.
insights.quote: What we do at the chip level is incredibly important, though, because that’s where the heat is being generated.
insights.locator: Big trade-offs in data centers — "We’re all basically on the same page here"

insights.claim: When multi-die packages are abstracted for tractability, the abstraction cannot be pushed so far that fidelity is lost in either static or dynamic thermal processing.
insights.speaker: Jack Berg, VP of business development, Silvaco
insights.so_what: Abstraction-versus-fidelity is the central technical trade in thermal EDA; tools that lose dynamic behavior will fail on real AI workloads.
insights.locator: Big trade-offs in data centers — "There are trade-offs at the chip level"

themes.theme: From PVT corners to per-transistor hotspots

insights.claim: Traditional thermal sign-off used three PVT corners — high, medium and low temperature — but customers now demand the temperature of a specific transistor and the exact location of hotspots so design changes can be made.
insights.speaker: Lang Lin, director of product management, Synopsys
insights.so_what: A step-change in required simulation resolution means far more compute per tapeout and a new upsell tier for EDA vendors.
insights.quote: Everybody is looking for the temperature of a specific transistor.
insights.locator: Where do you start — "You also need more accuracy and higher fidelity for the temperature"

insights.claim: The industry has solved per-gate resolution for voltage analysis — IR drop is in good shape at per-gate granularity — but has not achieved the equivalent per-gate thermal analysis.
insights.speaker: Lang Lin, director of product management, Synopsys
insights.so_what: Names the specific open capability gap in thermal EDA; the vendor that ships per-gate thermal first takes the sign-off slot.
insights.quote: IR drop is now in good shape, and we’re getting per-gate drop. But we haven’t done per-gate thermal.
insights.locator: Where do you start — "We have done that for voltage"

insights.claim: Hotspot locations shift depending on how the software running on the chip is written, so thermal cannot be treated as a purely hardware problem.
insights.speaker: Jack Berg, VP of business development, Silvaco
insights.so_what: Static thermal sign-off systematically understates risk for workload-diverse AI silicon — a hidden source of field failures.
insights.quote: Depending on how the software is developed, the hotspots can change. It’s not a straight hardware problem.
insights.locator: Where do you start — "Berg: Depending on how the software is developed"

insights.claim: A single package at the chip level may now contain 20 or 25 different chiplets, making it essential to understand thermal behavior inside the package with enough fidelity to guarantee reliability.
insights.speaker: Jack Berg, VP of business development, Silvaco
insights.so_what: A concrete complexity metric for advanced packages — 20-25 die per package sets the scale of the modeling problem vendors must solve.
insights.locator: Where do you start — "At the chip level, you may have 20 or 25 different chiplets"

insights.claim: The first consequence of inadequate thermal analysis is electromigration, followed by phase changes in materials that create reliability problems.
insights.speaker: Jack Berg, VP of business development, Silvaco
insights.so_what: Gives the specific failure chain to watch in high-density AI packages — electromigration is the early warning of thermal underdesign.
insights.quote: Typically, the first thing that happens when you don’t look at heat closely enough is you get electromigration.
insights.locator: Where do you start — "Understanding what’s happening inside the package is essential"

themes.theme: Packaging materials and cooling architecture shift

insights.claim: Materials innovation is concentrated on TIM 1 and TIM 2 thermal interface layers as suppliers try to break existing conductivity barriers.
insights.speaker: Satish Radhakrishnan, head of semiconductor and electronics, Vinci
insights.so_what: Thermal interface material suppliers sit on a specific, near-term materials bottleneck in AI packaging.
insights.locator: Where do you start — "For packaging, we’re seeing materials innovation with TIM 1 and TIM 2"

insights.claim: Cooling is moving from cooling the package lid to direct chip cooling, and immersion and two-phase cooling represent distinct architectures that will appear in the industry this year and next.
insights.speaker: Satish Radhakrishnan, head of semiconductor and electronics, Vinci
insights.so_what: A dated adoption call on cooling architecture transitions — a near-term catalyst window for liquid and two-phase cooling suppliers.
insights.quote: Immersive cooling and two-phase cooling are different architectures that you’ll be seeing in the industry this year and next year.
insights.locator: Where do you start — "The second part is the cooling itself"

insights.claim: Liquid cooling must be applied to the entire package rather than a single die, and removing heat from the package is a separate requirement on top of the cooling method itself.
insights.speaker: Satish Radhakrishnan, head of semiconductor and electronics, Vinci
insights.so_what: Package-level rather than die-level cooling raises the content value of cold plates and manifolds per accelerator.
insights.quote: It’s for the entire package. You need liquid cooling, plus you need to take the heat away.
insights.locator: Is that just for a single chip? — "Radhakrishnan: It’s for the entire package"

themes.theme: Thermal pressure reshaping memory and interconnect

insights.claim: ASIC accelerators are running hot enough that HBM is moving to custom HBM, shifting some power from the ASIC into the custom memory part — which raises the memory's temperature and creates new crosstalk to evaluate between the two.
insights.speaker: Satish Radhakrishnan, head of semiconductor and electronics, Vinci
insights.so_what: Thermal — not just bandwidth — is a driver of the custom HBM transition, which reshapes margin and design-win dynamics for memory makers.
insights.quote: The ASIC chips are getting so hot that HBM is going to custom HBM.
insights.locator: Where do you start — "Radhakrishnan: The ASIC chips are getting so hot"

insights.claim: Chiplet designers are splitting functions specifically along power lines and adopting co-packaged optics to bring networking closer, which forces evaluation of thermal crosstalk and of performance both per-die and as an integrated system.
insights.speaker: Satish Radhakrishnan, head of semiconductor and electronics, Vinci
insights.so_what: Power partitioning is becoming a chiplet design principle; co-packaged optics adds thermal risk that could gate its rollout.
insights.locator: Where do you start — "So with chiplets, people are splitting up functions in terms of power"

themes.theme: Reduced-order models, surrogates and digital twins

insights.claim: Computing accurate temperatures everywhere across a whole system is computationally very hard, so the emerging approach is a foundation model of a block or chiplet giving simplified thermal behavior, used to pre-compute and cut cost before running accurate simulation only on critical regions.
insights.speaker: Lang Lin, director of product management, Synopsys
insights.so_what: ML surrogates for physics simulation are the scaling path for thermal EDA — a concrete AI-in-EDA use case with measurable compute savings.
insights.quote: So you combine some fast, less-accurate model with a slow foundational model.
insights.locator: Where do you start — "To deal with a whole system and get accurate temperatures everywhere"

insights.claim: Techniques such as superposition and reduced-order modeling help thermal analysis scale, but the problem must be tackled at the architecture level so that end-of-flow verification does not force a design re-spin.
insights.speaker: Chris Mueth, director of new markets management, Keysight EDA
insights.so_what: Re-spin avoidance is the ROI argument for early thermal tooling — quantifiable against mask and schedule cost at advanced nodes.
insights.locator: Where do you start — "There are some techniques you can use, like superposition"

insights.claim: Architects need digital twin or surrogate models at chip level, package level and system level to make thermal trade-offs, and those surrogates must trace back to mechanical, thermal and electrical physics solvers that are consistent with one another.
insights.speaker: Jack Berg, VP of business development, Silvaco
insights.so_what: A three-tier digital twin stack is the stated architecture requirement — a roadmap checklist for evaluating multi-physics EDA vendors.
insights.locator: Where do you start — "Starting at the chip level and working up"

insights.claim: Making physics solvers consistent is a persistently nasty problem because each solver uses different partial differential equations that are cross-coupled to one another.
insights.speaker: Jack Berg, VP of business development, Silvaco
insights.so_what: Solver consistency is a deep technical moat — it explains why multi-physics leadership consolidates among a few large EDA vendors.
insights.quote: we’re talking about different physics solvers with different partial differential equations that are cross-coupled to each other
insights.locator: Where do you start — "That’s always a nasty issue"

insights.claim: Physics solvers come in three types — decoupled (pushing one physics into another), loosely coupled (iterative), and direct-coupled — and direct-coupled solvers handling stress and thermal simultaneously already exist and are required for chiplet package manufacturing problems such as thermal compression bonding.
insights.speaker: Chris Mueth, director of new markets management, Keysight EDA
insights.so_what: A precise capability test for thermal/mechanical tool vendors: direct-coupled stress-thermal is table stakes for advanced packaging assembly.
insights.quote: What you see out there are direct-coupled physics solvers that do stress and thermal at the same time.
insights.locator: Final exchange — "There are three types of physics solvers out there"

insights.claim: Multi-physics results must be brought together early and fast, which is pulling agentic Model Context Protocol approaches into thermal design flows despite AI being no more perfect than a human.
insights.speaker: Chris Mueth, director of new markets management, Keysight EDA
insights.so_what: MCP-based agentic orchestration is entering production EDA flows — an integration standard worth tracking across tool vendors.
insights.quote: AI is not perfect. It’s no more perfect than humans, and it can make mistakes just like humans.
insights.locator: Where do you start — "It all comes down to multi-physics"

insights.claim: The distinguishing risk of AI in design flows is not error rate but auditability, because a human cannot easily reconstruct an AI decision to find where the mistake was made.
insights.speaker: Chris Mueth, director of new markets management, Keysight EDA
insights.so_what: Explainability, not accuracy benchmarks, will determine how fast AI penetrates sign-off-grade EDA steps.
insights.quote: But it’s hard for a human to go back into a decision AI has made and figure out what mistakes it made.
insights.locator: Where do you start — "This is where the agentic MCP approach is coming in"

insights.claim: No single person can design a modern multi-die system, so tools must deliver role-scoped fidelity — full detail for the chip owner, coarser resolution for the package or system owner.
insights.speaker: Chris Mueth, director of new markets management, Keysight EDA
insights.so_what: Suggests seat-based, role-differentiated licensing for multi-physics tools rather than one monolithic product.
insights.quote: we can’t have one person design the whole thing. It’s impossible
insights.locator: Part of the solution is orchestration — "That’s an interesting problem from a design perspective"
